strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap at the intersection of continual learning and cooperative MARL, for which no dedicated benchmark previously existed.

The JAX-based, end-to-end GPU-accelerated implementation is a genuine engineering contribution: it enables training on sequences of up to 100 tasks in a few hours on a single desktop GPU, a large improvement in throughput over CPU-bound CL/MARL benchmarks (CORA, Continual World, COOM).

Procedural level generator with an explicit solvability validator (10 reachability/usability checks) provides a virtually unlimited, reproducible, and seed-controlled supply of tasks, mitigating overfitting to a fixed set of layouts.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation protocol: three complementary metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity), multiple CL baselines (FT, L2, EWC, Online EWC, MAS) combined with IPPO, and an ablation study isolating architectural factors (multi-head outputs, task ID, critic regularization, layer norm, CNN vs MLP).
The plasticity-loss experiment (repeating a task sequence multiple times) is a nice additional analysis connecting the CMARL setting to known single-agent continual RL pathologies.
Good documentation of implementation details in the appendix (generator algorithm, validator logic, upper-bound soup estimator, hyperparameters), which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The abstract and conclusion state that methods are shown to 'fail to scale to more complex settings' and that 'parameter-isolation methods fail to scale with longer task sequences,' but no parameter-isolation method (e.g., PackNet, mentioned in Related Work) is actually evaluated in the experiments; only regularization-based methods and naive fine-tuning are tested, creating a mismatch between claims and evidence.

The bulk of the detailed analysis (Figures 3-6, Table 2-3) is conducted only on Level 1 (easy) 20-task or 10-task sequences; Level 2 and Level 3 results are confined to a single appendix figure (Figure 7) with EWC only, so the central claim about performance degradation on harder settings is comparatively under-supported.

The domain remains narrow: all environments are variants of a single two-agent, fully-observable, discrete-action Overcooked-style kitchen. Despite the procedural generator, this limits the generality of conclusions about CMARL more broadly (e.g., no partial observability, no larger agent counts, no competitive or mixed-motive settings), a point the authors do acknowledge in Limitations.

Only one MARL backbone (IPPO) is evaluated, despite the Related Work section discussing VDN, QMIX, and MAPPO as alternative and potentially more coordination-aware algorithms; it is unclear whether the observed failure modes are specific to IPPO or general to MARL+CL combinations.

The task-incremental setting (task ID available during training) is the only continual learning paradigm studied, which is a relatively easy CL regime; more challenging class- or domain-incremental analogues for MARL are left entirely to future work.

The normalized scoring metric relies on a single-agent optimal cook-deliver cycle heuristic, which by the authors' own admission underestimates true throughput when multi-agent parallelization is possible, introducing potential noise/bias into cross-layout comparisons that is not empirically quantified.

No human-in-the-loop or zero-shot coordination evaluation is included despite the introduction motivating the work partly via human-AI coordination and autonomous vehicle scenarios, making the applied motivation somewhat disconnected from the actual experiments.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: no prior benchmark targets continual multi-agent RL specifically, and the paper clearly motivates why CMARL is harder than single-agent CL or static MARL (coordination breakdown, dual non-stationarity).

The JAX-based end-to-end GPU pipeline is a real practical contribution, enabling task sequences an order of magnitude longer (up to 100 tasks) than CPU-bound CRL benchmarks like Continual World or CORA, which is valuable for the community's ability to iterate quickly.

The procedural generation pipeline with a deterministic reachability/solvability validator (Appendix A.2-A.3) is well specified and reproducible, and allows a virtually unbounded supply of tasks controlled by a seed, mitigating overfitting to a fixed task set.

The evaluation protocol (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity) is sensible and the ablation study (multi-head outputs, task ID, critic regularization, layer norm, CNN vs. MLP) yields some concrete, if narrow, actionable findings for practitioners building CMARL agents.
Reasonably thorough documentation of hyperparameters, architecture choices, and metric definitions in the appendix supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Despite citing dedicated continual MARL methods (e.g., progressive task contextualization, [35]), the paper only evaluates generic single-agent CL methods (EWC, Online EWC, MAS, L2, FT) naively combined with IPPO. No multi-agent-aware CL baseline is implemented or compared, undermining the claim that the paper reveals fundamental CMARL-specific challenges rather than just restating known single-agent CL trade-offs (plasticity vs. stability) in a new domain.

Only IPPO is used as the underlying MARL algorithm, even though the related work section discusses VDN, QMIX, and MAPPO as relevant alternatives; the benchmark's claimed generality is not demonstrated across different MARL training paradigms.

The headline claim of scaling to 100-task sequences in the abstract/intro is not actually exercised in the main experiments — Table 2 and Figures 3/4 use only 20-task Level-1 (easy) sequences, and the plasticity study uses only 10-task sequences repeated. This creates a gap between the advertised capability and the demonstrated empirical contribution.

The core motivating scenarios (autonomous vehicles meeting new human drivers, warehouse robots adapting to new partners) emphasize changing partners/dynamics, yet MEAL's task sequences only vary static layout geometry — partner behavior and transition dynamics are not varied across tasks (acknowledged in Limitations but it weakens the paper's own motivation).

Difficulty-level results (Fig. 7, Appendix C.1) show all methods degrade substantially at Level 2/3, but only EWC is evaluated there; no analysis of which methods, if any, remain viable at harder difficulty, leaving the main scientific claim ('existing methods fail to scale to complex settings') under-supported by direct method comparison at higher difficulty.

Statistical support is modest: 5 seeds, with some metrics (e.g., MAS curves, ablation bars) showing wide confidence intervals, raising concerns about the robustness of some comparative claims (e.g., MAS ranking, layer-norm effect on L2).

The technical novelty of the environment itself is incremental, essentially a procedural-generation and task-sequencing wrapper around the existing JaxMARL Overcooked implementation, rather than a new environment family; this limits the contribution's originality relative to its 'first-of-its-kind' framing.

The single-agent-cycle-based normalization score (Appendix A.1) is an approximate heuristic that can misrepresent true task difficulty/upper bounds when two-agent parallelization is possible, and its impact on cross-layout comparisons is not empirically validated against ground-truth optimal multi-agent solutions.

The 'first' claims (first CMARL benchmark, first JAX continual RL library) are strong and should be tempered or more carefully substantiated given related efforts cited in the paper itself (e.g., JaxMARL, COOM).

strengths: Fills a clear gap: the first benchmark specifically targeting continual multi-agent RL (CMARL), an underexplored intersection of two active research areas.

End-to-end JAX implementation on top of JaxMARL/Overcooked provides substantial computational speedups (about 5 minutes per environment), enabling sequences of up to 100 tasks on a single GPU, far longer than prior CPU-bound CL benchmarks (5-15 tasks).

Procedural generation with a formal validator guarantees solvable, diverse layouts at controllable difficulty levels, giving a virtually unlimited task supply and reducing overfitting to a fixed set of environments, a meaningful methodological contribution beyond simply packaging existing tasks.

Reasonably thorough empirical study: multiple standard CL baselines (FT, L2, EWC, Online EWC, MAS) combined with IPPO, evaluated with three complementary metrics (average performance, forgetting, plasticity), plus a dedicated architecture ablation (multi-head, task ID, critic regularization, layer norm, CNN vs MLP) and a loss-of-plasticity study under task repetition.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendices specify the soup-delivery normalization metric, the procedural generation algorithm, the layout validator with explicit rules, network architecture, and hyperparameters, and code is released.
Honest and specific limitations section acknowledging scope restrictions (fully observable, two agents, discrete actions, only layout-based non-stationarity, no partner/dynamics shift).
weaknesses: The main baseline comparison (Table 2, Figure 3) is run on only a single 20-task Level 1 (easy) sequence; harder-level results are relegated to a single appendix figure (Fig. 7) without full metric tables (A, F, P) for Levels 2 and 3, limiting the evidence that the benchmark truly 'fails to scale' to harder settings as stated in the abstract.

No comparison against stronger or more recent CL methods beyond EWC/Online EWC/MAS/L2/FT; parameter-isolation methods such as PackNet are discussed in related work but never actually benchmarked, so the conclusion's claim that 'parameter-isolation methods fail to scale with longer task sequences' appears unsupported by the presented experiments.

The evaluation is restricted to the task-incremental setting with oracle task ID available at training; the more realistic task-agnostic/task-free continual setting is not explored, limiting the generality of conclusions about CMARL difficulty.

The ablation study (Figure 5) is conducted only on Level 1 10-task sequences, so it is unclear whether findings about architectural components (e.g., criticality of multi-head outputs) generalize to harder/longer sequences, where the benchmark's claimed scalability advantage would matter most.

The core environment family (Overcooked-style, two-agent, discrete, fully observable kitchens) is narrow relative to the broader motivating applications (autonomous vehicles, warehouse robots with many agents), and this gap between motivation and actual coverage is only partially addressed in the limitations.

The paper's novelty is primarily in benchmark engineering (JAX port, procedural generation, validator) rather than new algorithmic or theoretical insight into CMARL; despite heavy motivation around coordination breakdown and role forgetting in the introduction, the experiments mostly reconfirm known single-agent CL phenomena (stability-plasticity tradeoff, loss of plasticity) rather than isolating genuinely multi-agent-specific failure modes.

Statistical reporting is relatively thin: only 5 seeds, no significance testing beyond confidence intervals in plots, and some qualitative claims in the ablation discussion (e.g., critic regularization having 'negligible effect') are asserted from a single figure without deeper quantitative support.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap at the intersection of continual learning and cooperative MARL, with clear motivation and real-world analogies (AVs, warehouse robots).

The JAX-based, end-to-end GPU-accelerated pipeline is a valuable engineering contribution, enabling task sequences (up to 100 tasks) far longer than prior CPU-bound CL benchmarks (5-15 tasks), which should meaningfully lower the barrier to entry for CMARL research.

The procedural generation pipeline with a formal solvability validator (Appendix A.2-A.3) is well engineered and provides an effectively unbounded, reproducible (seed-controlled) task distribution rather than a fixed static set, addressing overfitting concerns raised by prior Overcooked robustness work.

Breadth of empirical investigation is impressive: six CL baselines across three difficulty levels, an architectural ablation (multi-head, task-ID, CNN vs MLP, critic regularization, layer norm), N-agent scaling (1-3 agents), network plasticity analysis via repetition, reward-design comparisons (shared/individual/sparse), partial observability, curriculum learning, and heterogeneous role assignment.

Principled normalization scheme (single-agent optimal cook-deliver cycle) allows comparison of normalized scores across heterogeneously sized/structured procedurally generated layouts, and continual learning metrics (average score, forgetting, forward transfer) are formally defined and computed with confidence intervals.
Extensive appendix detailing hyperparameters, network architecture, generator/validator pseudocode, and additional per-task curves supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built entirely on a single domain (Overcooked) with a single underlying MARL backbone (IPPO) for almost all main results; MAPPO and QMIX/VDN-style value-decomposition methods, which are standard in cooperative MARL, are only briefly touched (Section 5.7) rather than integrated as first-class baselines, limiting how representative the findings are for CMARL broadly despite the paper's benchmark framing.

Only the task-incremental setting (oracle task identity supplied at train and test time) is studied; this is an easier and less realistic CL protocol than task-agnostic/class-incremental settings, and the paper does not empirically probe how methods behave without this oracle signal, despite acknowledging it as a limitation.

Difficulty levels are defined by coarse heuristics (grid size ranges and obstacle density percentages) rather than a validated or continuous difficulty measure; the mapping from these surface statistics to 'coordination difficulty' is asserted rather than empirically justified (e.g., no correlation analysis between the chosen knobs and achieved task difficulty).

Many of the additional studies (curriculum learning, heterogeneous roles, reward design, N-agent) are single-setting demonstrations with only one sequence configuration and comparatively small sample sizes/high variance (e.g., Table 8 shows overlapping confidence intervals for the medium-difficulty comparison), so several conclusions are more suggestive than rigorously established.

Explanations for some counterintuitive findings (e.g., MAPPO underperforming IPPO under continual learning, Section 5.7) remain speculative ('a plausible cause...') without additional diagnostic experiments (e.g., analyzing critic value drift directly) to substantiate the proposed mechanism.

The normalized score's single-agent optimal-cycle upper bound is a heuristic approximation (ignoring two-agent parallelization) that can allow scores 'above 1'; while acknowledged, this makes cross-layout and cross-method comparisons somewhat approximate rather than exact, and the bound's tightness/looseness is not empirically validated against, e.g., a brute-force multi-agent optimum on small layouts.

The paper reports 5 seeds throughout; while confidence intervals are shown, some comparisons (e.g., EWC vs Online EWC on Level 2 in Table 11, CI ±0.34) have very wide intervals that undercut the strength of claims drawn from point-estimate rankings in the main text discussion.

As a resource/benchmark paper, the actual methodological contribution is limited to reimplementing six existing single-agent CL methods in JAX combined with IPPO; no new CMARL-specific algorithm is proposed, so the paper's value rests almost entirely on the benchmark's future adoption, which cannot be assessed at submission time.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored intersection (continual learning + cooperative MARL) and fills a clear gap in benchmark availability, as shown by the comparison table against CORA, Continual World, COOM, SMAC, etc.
JAX-based implementation enables much longer task sequences (up to 100 tasks) than prior CPU-bound CL benchmarks, which is a genuine practical contribution for the community.
The procedural generation pipeline with a formal solvability validator (10 rules, BFS/DFS-based) is well engineered and documented in detail, supporting reproducibility.

Very extensive empirical exploration: baseline CL methods (EWC, Online EWC, MAS, L2, AGEM, FT), architectural ablations (multi-head, task-ID, CNN vs MLP, layer norm), N-agent scaling, partial observability, reward design, designated roles, curriculum learning, and plasticity loss.
Reasonably clear writing and metric definitions (normalized score, forgetting, forward transfer) grounded in prior CL literature conventions.
Honest limitations section acknowledging narrow domain, discrete-only actions, and restriction to layout-only non-stationarity.
weaknesses: The notion of 'task diversity' is fairly shallow: all tasks are procedurally generated Overcooked kitchens that differ only in grid size/wall density/station placement, not in qualitatively different dynamics, objectives, or reward structures; this limits how representative the benchmark is of real continual-learning challenges (e.g., it is unclear whether an 'infinite' stream of superficially similar layouts meaningfully stresses catastrophic forgetting versus simple interpolation).

Scientific contribution is primarily an engineering combination of existing components (JaxMARL's Overcooked, existing single-agent CL regularization methods, IPPO) rather than a new method or deep new understanding; no architecture- or replay-based CL baselines beyond AGEM (e.g., PackNet, mentioned in related work, is never implemented or compared).

The core evaluation metric relies on a heuristic single-agent optimal cook-deliver cycle as the normalizer, which the authors admit underestimates multi-agent throughput; this makes normalized scores (sometimes >1, sometimes clustering near 0.1–0.3 on harder levels) difficult to interpret cleanly as indicators of coordination quality versus artifacts of the bound's looseness.

Several secondary studies (N-agent scaling, partial observability, reward design, designated roles) are based on single configurations/limited seeds with large or unreported confidence intervals in places (e.g., Table 11's EWC row has A=0.604±0.21), making some conclusions (e.g., about MAPPO underperforming IPPO, or 2 vs 3 agents) only weakly supported statistically.

Difficulty levels are defined by coarse, somewhat arbitrary heuristics (width/height ranges and obstacle density percentages) rather than a principled difficulty metric, and only three discrete levels are provided, limiting fine-grained scaling studies.

The claimed novelty of being the 'first end-to-end GPU-accelerated' CL library is slightly overstated given CORA is already listed as GPU-accelerated in Table 1 (albeit single-agent), so the precise novel claim should be narrowed to the multi-agent setting.

Despite extensive breadth, the depth of analysis for each sub-study is shallow (often a single table/figure with brief qualitative explanation), giving the impression of a broad survey of ablations rather than rigorous, well-controlled experiments driving toward actionable insights or new algorithmic recommendations.

strengths: Addresses a clearly underexplored but important intersection (continual learning + cooperative MARL) and provides the first dedicated benchmark for it, with a concrete and well-motivated comparison table (Table 1) against existing CL and MARL benchmarks.

The JAX-based, end-to-end GPU-accelerated implementation is a genuine engineering contribution: it enables training over sequences of up to 100 tasks on a single desktop GPU, which is a substantial practical improvement over CPU-bound CL benchmarks limited to 5-15 tasks.

The procedural generation pipeline with a formally specified validator (reachability/usability checks, Appendix A.2-A.3) is a principled way to produce an effectively unbounded, solvable task distribution, avoiding overfitting to a fixed set of layouts that plagues prior CL benchmarks.

The empirical study is extensive and goes well beyond a simple baseline table: six CL methods are evaluated across three difficulty levels, complemented by architectural ablations, an N-agent extension (1-3 agents), partial observability variants, reward-design comparisons, curriculum learning, and a dedicated plasticity-loss study. This breadth gives a multi-faceted picture of what currently works and fails in CMARL.

Several findings are genuinely informative and non-obvious, e.g., the EWC vs. Online EWC stability-plasticity trade-off that flips with difficulty level, the critical importance of multi-head output architectures, and the counter-intuitive underperformance of MAPPO relative to IPPO under continual learning with partial observability — these provide useful signposts for future method development.

Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, pseudocode for the generator/validator/upper-bound calculator, and seeds are reported, and the paper states code/environments are released.
weaknesses: The benchmark is entirely built on a single environment family (procedurally varied Overcooked layouts). Despite the claim of 'infinite' tasks, all tasks share identical dynamics, action space, and objective structure, so conclusions about CMARL may not generalize to other environment families or task structures (e.g., varying dynamics, partner identity, or reward functions, as the paper itself admits in the Limitations section).

Difficulty levels are defined through simple geometric heuristics (grid size, obstacle density) rather than through a more principled or validated difficulty metric; the claim that these levels correspond to meaningfully different coordination demands is supported mainly post hoc by observing that scores decrease, which is somewhat circular reasoning.

Only IPPO (and MAPPO in one partial-observability ablation) is used as the underlying MARL algorithm; despite VDN/QMIX being discussed in related work, no value-decomposition based baselines are evaluated, leaving open whether the observed phenomena (e.g., forgetting/plasticity patterns) are specific to independent actor-critic methods.

Several results show large confidence intervals (e.g., Level 2 EWC average score 0.604±0.21), and only 5 seeds are used, which limits the statistical reliability of some comparative claims, particularly in the harder difficulty levels where most methods perform poorly.

The single-agent optimal cook-deliver cycle used to normalize scores is a heuristic upper bound that ignores multi-agent parallelization; its use as a basis for interpreting scores above 1.0 as 'effective cooperation' is reasonable but somewhat approximate, and the paper does not validate how tight or loose this bound is across difficulty levels.

The study evaluates only the task-incremental setting (task identity known at train/test time), which is an easier and less realistic CL regime than task-agnostic settings; this restricts the practical implications of the findings for more realistic continual deployment scenarios.

No comparison is made with CMARL-specific methods from the literature that the paper itself cites (e.g., progressive task contextualization), so the evaluation mainly repurposes single-agent CL techniques rather than testing against the small existing body of CMARL-specific solutions, limiting the paper's ability to claim it identifies genuine gaps relative to the state of the art in CMARL specifically.
